summary:
San Marino is workable for trans visitors: safe in practice, thin in law. Consensual same-sex relations were decriminalised in 2004, no legal penalty attaches to gender identity, and no statute regulates which bathrooms or facilities a person may use. No pattern of anti-trans violence is documented in this small, tourism-dependent country, and entry carries no documented friction — the border with Italy is open, with no recorded identity screening that risks outing an arriving visitor.

Legal gender recognition does not exist. The 2026 edition of the ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map lists San Marino among the countries with no functioning legal or administrative process for changing gender markers. The consequence falls on residents rather than travellers: a visitor's foreign documents govern throughout, and there is no domestic procedure that could alter them during a stay.

Constitutional anti-discrimination protection is anchored in sexual orientation. In a referendum held on 4 June 2019, Sammarinese voters approved inserting a clause prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation into the constitution. The sources assembled here do not record a parallel clause covering gender identity or gender expression.

Relationship recognition is in place. The legislature approved a civil-unes union law in November 2018, reported at the time as leaner than Italy's Cirinnà statute, and legal recognition of gay couples is dated to 2016 in other reporting. Partner recognition therefore exists, though it is framed for same-sex couples rather than as a trans-specific protection.

San Marino has engaged international protection machinery. It was one of twelve states examined at the 34th session of the Universal Periodic Review Working Group in November 2019, and ILGA has compiled the SOGIESC recommendations put to each state examined in that round, including San Marino, together with the responses. The individual recommendations are not reproduced in the material available here.

The overall picture for a visitor is very high de facto safety with minimal explicit legal infrastructure for trans people. No legal exposure is documented for a traveller, and the gaps identified — the absent gender-recognition process and the orientation-only constitutional clause — are resident-facing rather than border-facing.
tangentialFactors:
The wider political climate reads as tolerant rather than trans-specific. Reporting on Paolo Rondelli's appointment as captain regent on 4 April 2022, the world's first openly gay head of state serving a six-month term with no executive power, notes that homosexuality remained punishable by jail time in San Marino until 2004 and that legal recognition of gay couples followed in 2016. The trajectory is one of steady liberalisation on orientation grounds, with gender identity not yet a named category in the constitutional text.

Regional comparison is unflattering on documents. The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 chapter on legal gender recognition records 2025 country-by-country developments across Europe, among them Albania's rejection of a self-ID recommendation at its Universal Periodic Review, legal action brought by trans activist Luana Myrto, and Andorra's delayed hormone-treatment decree. San Marino generates no comparable entry: neighbouring and peer jurisdictions have active litigation, decrees and contested reforms, while San Marino has no process for these disputes to arise over.

Scale shapes the risk profile. San Marino is a microstate whose economy leans heavily on tourism, which raises the practical cost of any hostile incident and reduces the anonymity-driven friction a trans visitor might encounter elsewhere.
localsOnly:
Residents have no route to amend the gender marker on official documents. The ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map's 2026 legal-gender-recognition category places San Marino among the states with no functioning legal or administrative procedure, so identity papers, civil records and the interactions that depend on them remain fixed as issued.

Residents are covered by a constitutional prohibition on discrimination grounded in sexual orientation, approved by referendum on 4 June 2019. Whether that clause is invoked on behalf of gender identity is not addressed by the sources here.

Same-sex couples may register their relationship. The civil-unes union law approved by the legislature in November 2018 provides the framework in force, described in reporting as leaner than the Cirinnà statute of the neighbouring country, with recognition of gay couples dated to 2016.

The state has submitted to international review. At the 34th session of the Universal Periodic Review Working Group in November 2019 it was one of twelve countries examined, receiving SOGIESC recommendations that ILGA has compiled alongside each state's responses.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether San Marino's 2019 constitutional clause against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation extends to gender identity or gender expression. The sources establish the orientation wording only, and no separate gender-identity provision is recorded here.

Unresolved: the dating of relationship recognition. One source places legal recognition of gay couples in 2016, another records legislative approval of the civil-unes union law in November 2018; whether these mark different stages of the same reform is not settled by the material available.

Unresolved: the content of the SOGIESC recommendations San Marino received at its November 2019 Universal Periodic Review and which of them the state accepted. The compilation is referenced but the individual recommendations and responses are not reproduced.

Not sourced: any data on enforcement of the constitutional clause, on hate-crime offences motivated by gender identity, or on access to trans-specific healthcare for short-term visitors. The absence of documented anti-trans violence reflects an absence of reporting rather than a verified count.

The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 findings cited in the comparison concern Albania and Andorra, not San Marino; the review's San Marino content is limited to the country's placement in the no-process category.
